introduction: “Among the people are those who have heard the Call and turned towards it, and among them are those who heard and turned away, and among them are those who did not hear.” With small variations that sentence recurs through the hundred quotations kept here, most of them from tablets of Bahá’u’lláh. Around it the readings observe who responds and who does not: the learned are often prevented and the unlettered accept; rank in a former Revelation counts for nothing in the next; hesitation and wavering are treated as forms of denial; trials sift the steadfast; and the two outcomes are called certitude and doubt, wine drunk and wine refused, life and death, sight and blindness. The Gospels and the Qur’án record the same division in nearly the same words, and most of the outside quotations are theirs: the sower, the new wine, “let the dead bury their dead,” “a wizard or a madman,” “it is not the eyes that grow blind.” The contrasts come from within the same scriptures as well as outside them: “no compulsion in religion” and “unto you your religion”; the wheat and tares left to grow together; “he that is not against us is on our part”; the Pharisee who thanked God he was not as other men; Gamaliel, Tennyson, Clifford and Mill on the uses of doubt.
questions: “How many a learned one was prevented, and how many a handmaiden heard.” Why should learning and standing so often be obstacles, and what in you plays their part?
The readings treat hesitation as denial; Gamaliel counselled waiting, and Tennyson honoured “honest doubt.” How would you tell honest inquiry from evasion in yourself?
“He who hath not heard is counted among the dead.” Jesus and the Qur’án use the same language. What is the life that is meant, and how should one speak of those who do not share it?
The Qur’án says “there is no compulsion in religion” and the parable leaves wheat and tares to the harvest. What conduct toward those who turn away do these readings, read together with them, allow?
“Those who have believed today … are among the most excellent of creation.” What keeps this from becoming the Pharisee’s prayer?
The father’s prayer, “I believe; help thou mine unbelief,” fits neither side of the division. What place do the readings on trial and steadfastness give to a believer who is still struggling?

outside.why: Some heard the Call and turned to it, some heard and turned away, some did not hear. Luke’s report of Paul’s last audience in Rome: some believed the things which were spoken, and some believed not.
Jesus described the same three and four outcomes as soils: some seeds fell by the way side, some upon stony places, some among thorns, but other fell into good ground.
“Faith is of two kinds”: of the tongue, and of the heart. The Qur’án to the desert Arabs: say “We submit,” for the faith hath not yet entered into your hearts.

Why do not all hear and obey? The Qur’án: if thy Lord willed, all who are in the earth would have believed together. Wouldst thou compel men until they are believers? What does a faith that cannot be compelled require of the one who calls to it?
“His remembrance of His servants hath ever preceded their remembrance of Him.” The letter to Laodicea: behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice.
Pascal hears the same priority: thou wouldst not seek Me, if thou hadst not found Me.
“Not every ear heareth.” Jesus ends his parables with it: he that hath ears to hear, let him hear.
“How many a learned one was prevented, and how many a handmaiden heard.” Jesus: thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes.
The mature deprived, the suckling fed. Paul to Corinth: not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called.
The psalm the image comes from: out of the mouth of babes and sucklings hast thou ordained strength.
Souls occupied day and night with God’s commandments, “nevertheless their deeds were not accepted.” Jesus to the chief priests: the publicans and the harlots go into the kingdom of God before you.
The elder brother’s complaint is theirs: lo, these many years do I serve thee, neither transgressed I at any time thy commandment. What had his years of service not given him?
“If you say there is confusion … then come forth to hear and see.” The questioners in the Temple: how long dost thou make us to doubt? If thou be the Christ, tell us plainly.

“In the station of certitude, doubt has no place.” Tennyson: there lives more faith in honest doubt, believe me, than in half the creeds. Is the doubt Tennyson honours the doubt these readings condemn?
Divines who miss the Day of Reckoning are “branded as guilty of folly.” The Pharisees’ argument against Jesus: have any of the rulers or of the Pharisees believed on him?
“How many a one robed in authority hath disdained.” John on those who did not disdain and still held back: they loved the praise of men more than the praise of God.
“The call of the oneness of humanity has been sounded.” Hebrews: to day if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts.
One cried “the Apostle of God,” another “he hath fabricated.” The Qur’án: there came no messenger unto those before them but they said: A wizard or a madman!
The reading quotes this verse for those who responded: Our Lord! Lo! we have heard a crier calling unto Faith: “Believe ye in your Lord!” So we believed.
And the Qur’án’s account of those who “persisted”: if they saw every token they would not believe therein; they say, This is naught else than fables of the men of old.
“In every age there have been and will be the truthful and the false.” Stephen before the council: which of the prophets have not your fathers persecuted?
Belonging to a former Revelation is no proof in the next. Jesus: had ye believed Moses, ye would have believed me; for he wrote of me.
The highest in the Bayán may become “a letter of negation.” John the Baptist: think not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father.
Jesus met the same claim of descent and answered it by conduct: if ye were Abraham’s children, ye would do the works of Abraham.
“The loftiest Tree of affirmation … becometh lower than the most inferior tree of negation.” Jesus: the last shall be first, and the first last.
“The most abject of men” may be among the people of abiding life. Simeon over the infant Jesus: this child is set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel.

“If you believe not in Me, you have not believed in any of the Messengers.” An early chapter of the Qur’án ends its address to unbelievers differently: unto you your religion, and unto me my religion. Can a claim be absolute and its manner of address still leave others free?
“Whoso turneth away this Day hath in truth turned away from God from time immemorial.” John: he came unto his own, and his own received him not.
“Whoso hesitateth in this Cause.” Elijah on Carmel: how long halt ye between two opinions? And the people answered him not a word.
Gamaliel, a teacher of the law, advised exactly the hesitation the reading condemns: refrain from these men, and let them alone. When is waiting to see wisdom, and when is it refusal?
Those who “turned away or hesitated.” Athens after Paul’s speech: some mocked: and others said, We will hear thee again of this matter.
Vain imaginings, a name, desires: each keeps someone back. The guests invited to the great supper: they all with one consent began to make excuse.

Some turned “detached from all,” others were “content with their own vain imaginings.” Jesus: wide is the gate that leadeth to destruction; strait is the gate which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it.
“How many a soul … hath turned away and followed every envious opponent.” Jerusalem at the feast: some said, He is a good man: others said, Nay; but he deceiveth the people.
Those who “turned upon their heels.” Jesus: no man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.
Souls who “incline with every wind and are moved by every fancy.” James: he that wavereth is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed.
“Shame upon those who believed then disbelieved, drew near then withdrew.” The Qur’án: those who believe, then disbelieve and then again believe, then disbelieve.
John on those who left his own community: they went out from us, but they were not of us.
“At times we find thee repentant … at other times we see thee an unbeliever.” The Qur’án: swaying between this and that, belonging neither to these nor to those.
The letter to Laodicea has no patience with a faith that will not settle either way: I would thou wert cold or hot.
Guidance and “manifest error.” The Qur’án joins the clear distinction to a clear prohibition: there is no compulsion in religion. The right direction is henceforth distinct from error.
Some “acted according to what was ordained.” The Qur’án: be not as those who say, we hear, and they hear not.

“We have commanded all to that which profiteth them. Some have turned towards it and some have turned away.” The Qur’án sets the limit of the messenger’s task: thou art a warner only. What does that limit ask of believers when others turn away?
The traveller is “now lifted up to heaven, now cast into the depths.” Peter walked on the water toward Jesus; but when he saw the wind boisterous, he was afraid, and began to sink.
“Through trials and afflictions are the steadfast distinguished from the doubters.” The Qur’án: do men imagine that they will be left at ease because they say, We believe, and will not be tested?
And its portrait of the one who fails: he worshippeth Allah upon a narrow marge, so that if a trial befalleth him, he falleth away utterly.
Steadfastness and sacrifice are “not the work of every soul.” When many of his disciples went back, Jesus asked the twelve: will ye also go away? Peter: to whom shall we go?
“The beginning of the Cause is belief in God, and its end is steadfastness in His love.” Jesus: he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved.

“Cast aside doubts and idle fancies.” A father in the Gospel could only do half of it, and said so: Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief. He was answered. Where does his prayer belong in the readings’ division of the certain and the doubting?
“This is the Day wherein the eye of doubt hath been blinded.” Jesus to Thomas, offering the evidence he had asked for: be not faithless, but believing.

“Those who doubted are wandering in the wilderness of heedlessness.” W. K. Clifford made doubt a duty: it is wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone, to believe anything upon insufficient evidence. What evidence do the readings offer the doubter, and where is he told to look for it?
“The sincere ones are certain of the meeting with their Lord.” Jesus: blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed.
“Every assured one hath drunk.” Isaiah’s invitation is to all: ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money.
“The choice wine of certitude.” Jesus on what a new vintage requires: they put new wine into new bottles, and both are preserved.
And on why it is refused: no man also having drunk old wine straightway desireth new: for he saith, The old is better.
The wine of life is offered “upon all who dwell in the realm of possibility.” Proverbs: Wisdom crieth without; she uttereth her voice in the streets.
That the Word “detach thee from all who are on earth.” The merchant in the parable: when he had found one pearl of great price, he went and sold all that he had, and bought it.
One who “believed when most of the people have disbelieved.” Jesus: fear not, little flock.
A servant who “walked in the path of certitude until he … recognized.” The man born blind, pressed by the authorities: one thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see.
“Blessed art thou for having believed.” Jesus to his disciples: blessed are your eyes, for they see: many prophets and righteous men have desired to see those things which ye see.
“Among the handmaidens are those who have heard and turned towards God.” A Samaritan woman was the first to bring her town: many believed on him for the saying of the woman.

Those who turned away “are in grievous loss.” The householder in the parable forbids his servants to do the sorting: nay; lest while ye gather up the tares, ye root up also the wheat. Let both grow together until the harvest. Who, in the readings, does the distinguishing?
He who turned “hath verily become one of those drawn nigh.” James: draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you.
“Hearken unto the counsel of this compassionate Counsellor.” Jesus: my sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.
Some denied, some “turned towards His straight path.” Joshua at Shechem: choose you this day whom ye will serve.
Some “rejected the signs of God,” others “hastened.” John’s explanation: light is come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light.

“Some were drawn to it … while others heard and turned away.” John: there was a division among them for these sayings. Many said, He hath a devil; others said, These are not the words of him that hath a devil.
Whoever turns away “has lost in this world and the next.” Jesus: what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?
Nearness or opposition, recorded “in God’s Book.” Moses: I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life.

“Those who have believed today, they are among the most excellent of creation.” Jesus told a story about a man who knew he was among the excellent: God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are. How is a believer to hear this reading without praying that prayer?
Those who turned to Him are “among the people of Paradise.” Jesus: he that heareth my word, and believeth, is passed from death unto life.
“There is naught between negation and affirmation.” Jesus: he that is not with me is against me.
And yet, of a stranger who worked in his name without joining the disciples: forbid him not; for he that is not against us is on our part. How can both sayings be true, and which applies when?
“We behold thee wavering between two paths.” Proverbs: turn not to the right hand nor to the left: remove thy foot from evil.
God distinguishes “between light and darkness, through a word.” Jesus: think not that I am come to send peace on earth: I came not to send peace, but a sword.
“The peoples shall differ regarding this Ancient Light.” Paul: unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness.
Two calls are raised, and many answer the wrong one. Jesus: the stone which the builders rejected, the same is become the head of the corner.
The deniers said, “We hear and we disobey.” The words are from the Qur’án’s account of Sinai: they said: We hear and we rebel.
“He who hath not heard is counted among the dead.” The Qur’án to Muhammad: thou canst not make the dead to hear, nor canst thou make the deaf to hear the call when they have turned to flee.
Moses, after forty years with his people: yet the Lord hath not given you an heart to perceive, and eyes to see, and ears to hear, unto this day.
“They who have disbelieved—these are the dead.” Jesus used the word the same way: let the dead bury their dead.

If they find the path of God “they take it not for their path.” The Qur’án: having hearts wherewith they understand not, and having eyes wherewith they see not, and having ears wherewith they hear not.
“Think not that they who turned away are alive.” Paul to those who had turned: you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins.
The veiled are “dead servants”; those who drank living waters live. The Qur’án: is he who was dead and We have raised him unto life, as him whose similitude is in utter darkness?

Whoever turns away “is verily among the dead.” The Qur’án says of such: Allah hath sealed their hearing and their hearts. If the dead cannot hear and the sealed cannot open, in what sense is turning away a choice? How do the readings hold a person responsible?
Faces illumined “by the lights of the Countenance.” Peter: who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light.
The weak of sight “like bats, crept into the cave of darkness.” Plato: human beings living in an underground den, who see only the shadows on the wall and take them for the truth.
They ask “Where is the light?” and so “proclaim their blindness.” Jesus: if ye were blind, ye should have no sin: but now ye say, We see; therefore your sin remaineth.
The Qur’án: it is not the eyes that grow blind, but it is the hearts, which are within the bosoms, that grow blind.
“The blind are in veil … and say: Where is the Sun?” Jesus: they seeing see not; and hearing they hear not, neither do they understand.
Those with sight “received their portion.” Isaiah was sent knowing the other result: hear ye indeed, but understand not; and see ye indeed, but perceive not.
The Qur’án’s shortest verse on those who would not look, which gives the reason they stay as they are: deaf, dumb and blind; and they return not.
What can the worm know of the morning breeze, or the owl of the rose garden? Jesus: neither cast ye your pearls before swine.
The nightingale’s song is “abhorrent to crow and raven.” Paul: to the one we are the savour of death unto death; and to the other the savour of life unto life.
The same fragrance delights one creature and repels another. Abraham in the parable: if they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead.

“These are believers, those are deniers; these are luminous, those are in darkness.” John Stuart Mill: he who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that. What would it mean to know the denier’s side while holding one’s own?

“One raised the cry of joy while another wailed in despair.” Jesus on a generation that would accept neither: we have piped unto you, and ye have not danced; we have mourned unto you, and ye have not lamented.
“Woe betide him who hath followed vain imaginings after the Sun of Certitude hath shone.” John: every one that doeth evil hateth the light.
A servant who “hath abandoned superstitions, emerged from darkness.” The Qur’án knows the counterfeit of that claim: of mankind are some who say: We believe, when they believe not.
The guide ends in prayer. The psalmist’s, for the same gift of sight: open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law.

quran-a-crier-calling-unto-faith.text: Our Lord! Lo! we have heard a crier calling unto Faith: "Believe ye in your Lord!" So we believed. Our Lord! Therefor forgive us our sins, and remit from us our evil deeds, and make us die the death of the righteous.

quran-we-hear-and-we-rebel.text: And when We made with you a covenant and caused the Mount to tower above you, (saying): Hold fast by that which We have given you, and hear (Our Word), they said: We hear and we rebel. And (worship of) the calf was made to sink into their hearts because of their rejection (of the covenant). Say (unto them): Evil is that which your belief enjoineth on you, if ye are believers.

quran-canst-not-make-the-dead-to-hear.text: Lo! thou canst not make the dead to hear, nor canst thou make the deaf to hear the call when they have turned to flee;

quran-wouldst-thou-compel-men.text: And if thy Lord willed, all who are in the earth would have believed together. Wouldst thou (Muhammad) compel men until they are believers?

quran-believe-then-disbelieve.text: Lo! those who believe, then disbelieve and then (again) believe, then disbelieve, and then increase in disbelief, Allah will never pardon them, nor will He guide them unto a way.

quran-upon-a-narrow-marge.text: And among mankind is he who worshippeth Allah upon a narrow marge so that if good befalleth him he is content therewith, but if a trial befalleth him, he falleth away utterly. He loseth both the world and the Hereafter. That is the sheer loss.

quran-swaying-between-this-and-that.text: Swaying between this (and that), (belonging) neither to these nor to those. He whom Allah causeth to go astray, thou (O Muhammad) wilt not find a way for him:

quran-fables-of-the-men-of-old.text: Of them are some who listen unto thee, but We have placed upon their hearts veils, lest they should understand, and in their ears a deafness. If they saw every token they would not believe therein; to the point that, when they come unto thee to argue with thee, the disbelievers say: This is naught else than fables of the men of old.

quran-sealed-their-hearing.text: Allah hath sealed their hearing and their hearts, and on their eyes there is a covering. Theirs will be an awful doom.

acts-some-believed-and-some-believed-not.text: And some believed the things which were spoken, and some believed not

acts-some-mocked-and-others-said.text: And when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked: and others said, We will hear thee again of this matter. So Paul departed from among them. Howbeit certain men clave unto him, and believed

john-murmuring-among-the-people.text: And there was much murmuring among the people concerning him: for some said, He is a good man: others said, Nay; but he deceiveth the people

john-my-sheep-hear.text: My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me
